questions.q: Which basophilic cytoplasmic granules found in the neuronal soma and dendrites (but absent from the axon hillock and axon) consist of stacks of rough endoplasmic reticulum and polyribosomes?
questions.explain: Nissl bodies are abundant aggregates of rough endoplasmic reticulum and free polyribosomes in the perikaryon and proximal dendrites that synthesize neuronal proteins; their absence from the axon hillock helps identify the axon origin histologically.

open.q: Name the basophilic clumps of rough endoplasmic reticulum and polyribosomes present in the neuronal cell body and dendrites but absent from the axon hillock.

questions.q: Which structural class of neuron possesses a single short process bifurcating into peripheral and central axons and is found in dorsal root ganglia and cranial nerve sensory ganglia?
questions.explain: Pseudounipolar neurons develop from bipolar neuroblasts whose two processes fuse near the soma, forming a T-shaped single process; they are the primary somatic and visceral sensory neurons in spinal and cranial ganglia.

open.q: Which structural type of neuron is characteristic of dorsal root ganglia and sensory ganglia of cranial nerves?

questions.q: Where in the adult human nervous system are true bipolar neurons normally located?
options: Retina, olfactory epithelium, and vestibular/cochlear ganglia
Dorsal root ganglia and autonomic ganglia
Anterior horn of the spinal cord and cerebral cortex
Sympathetic chain ganglia and adrenal medulla
questions.explain: True bipolar neurons have one dendrite and one axon arising from opposite poles of the soma and are restricted to special sensory pathways: retinal bipolar cells, olfactory receptor neurons, and spiral/vestibular ganglion cells.

open.q: Name two anatomical sites in the adult human body where bipolar neurons are found.

questions.q: Which molecular motor protein mediates fast retrograde axonal transport from the axon terminal back toward the neuronal cell body (perikaryon)?
questions.explain: Microtubules in axons are polarized with minus ends toward the soma and plus ends toward the terminal; cytoplasmic dynein drives retrograde transport toward the soma (used by neurotrophic factors and herpes/rabies viruses), whereas kinesin drives anterograde transport.

open.q: Name the microtubule-associated motor protein responsible for retrograde axonal transport toward the neuronal soma.

questions.q: What triggers the fusion of neurotransmitter-containing synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic active zone membrane when an action potential reaches the axon terminal?
options: Influx of calcium ions through voltage-gated calcium channels
Efflux of potassium ions through leak channels
Influx of chloride ions through GABA-A receptors
questions.explain: Depolarization of the presynaptic bouton opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels; the resulting Ca2+ influx binds synaptotagmin, activating SNARE proteins to mediate synaptic vesicle exocytosis.

open.q: Influx of which divalent cation into the presynaptic axon terminal triggers synaptic vesicle exocytosis?

questions.q: Which CNS macroglial cell forms perivascular end-feet around brain capillaries as part of the blood-brain barrier, buffers extracellular potassium, and expresses glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)?
questions.explain: Astrocytes are star-shaped neuroectoderm-derived glial cells with radiating processes ending in vascular end-feet (glia limitans), regulating extracellular ions, neurotransmitter reuptake, and glial scar formation; GFAP is their specific immunohistochemical marker.

open.q: Name the star-shaped CNS glial cell that forms perivascular end-feet and expresses glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP).

questions.q: Which glial cell produces and maintains the myelin sheaths around multiple axons simultaneously within the central nervous system?
questions.explain: Each oligodendrocyte extends multiple tongue-like processes that wrap concentrically around segments of up to 30 to 50 different axons in the CNS, whereas each Schwann cell myelinates only a single internode of one axon in the PNS.

open.q: Which CNS neuroglial cell wraps myelin sheaths around multiple axons simultaneously?

questions.q: Unlike neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes (which arise from neuroectoderm), from which embryonic origin are CNS resident phagocytic microglia derived?
questions.explain: Microglia originate from mesodermal yolk sac myeloid progenitors that migrate into the developing neural tube early in embryogenesis, functioning as the resident macrophages and antigen-presenting cells of the CNS.

open.q: From which embryonic germ layer and progenitor lineage do CNS microglial cells originate?

questions.q: Which simple cuboidal-to-columnar ciliated glial cells line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord?
questions.explain: Ependymal cells form a single epithelial-like lining of the brain ventricles and spinal central canal, bearing apical cilia and microvilli that circulate cerebrospinal fluid; modified ependymal cells cover the vascular stroma of the choroid plexus.

open.q: Name the ciliated neuroglial cells that line the cerebral ventricles and the central canal of the spinal cord.

questions.q: Which structural component forms the primary anatomical diffusion barrier of the blood-brain barrier (BBB)?
options: Tight junctions between continuous capillary endothelial cells
questions.explain: The primary physical barrier of the BBB is formed by complex tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) sealing the clefts between continuous, non-fenestrated brain capillary endothelial cells, induced and maintained by pericytes and astrocytic end-feet.

open.q: Which intercellular junction between continuous brain capillary endothelial cells forms the physical seal of the blood-brain barrier?

questions.sub: Peripheral Nervous System Glia and Myelin
questions.q: From which embryonic structure do Schwann cells and ganglionic satellite cells of the peripheral nervous system arise?
questions.explain: All peripheral nervous system glial cells—Schwann cells (neurolemmocytes) and satellite cells surrounding ganglionic neuronal somata—are derived from the embryonic neural crest.

open.q: Which transient embryonic structure gives rise to both Schwann cells and ganglionic satellite cells in the peripheral nervous system?

questions.sub: Peripheral Nervous System Glia and Myelin
questions.q: What are the small, oblique funnel-shaped clefts within compact PNS myelin sheaths that retain Schwann cell cytoplasm and permit metabolic exchange across the myelin lamellae?
questions.explain: Schmidt-Lanterman clefts are narrow cytoplasmic channels trapped between compacted layers of Schwann cell myelin membrane, allowing continuity between the outer and inner Schwann cell cytoplasm.

open.q: Name the oblique cytoplasmic channels within peripheral myelin sheaths that maintain continuity between the inner and outer Schwann cell cytoplasm.

questions.sub: Peripheral Nervous System Glia and Myelin
questions.q: Why does saltatory conduction occur along myelinated axons?
options: Na+ channels cluster at nodes of Ranvier, enabling saltatory conduction
questions.explain: Myelin acts as a high-resistance, low-capacitance insulator across internodes while voltage-gated Na+ channels cluster densely at the nodes of Ranvier, enabling rapid node-to-node depolarization.

open.q: Name the periodic unmyelinated gaps along a myelinated axon where voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated for saltatory conduction.

questions.q: From outermost to innermost, what is the correct order of the three connective tissue sheaths of a peripheral nerve?
questions.explain: Dense irregular connective tissue (epineurium) binds multiple nerve fascicles together; specialized squamous-like epithelioid myofibroblasts (perineurium) enclose each fascicle; and loose reticular connective tissue (endoneurium) surrounds individual axons and Schwann cells.

open.q: List the three connective tissue investments of a peripheral nerve in order from superficial (outer) to deep (inner).

questions.q: Which peripheral nerve connective tissue layer consists of concentric layers of flattened epithelioid myofibroblasts joined by tight junctions that form the blood-nerve barrier?
questions.explain: The perineurium surrounds each nerve fascicle with concentric sleeves of flattened barrier cells sealed by zonulae occludentes, protecting the endoneurial microenvironment as the blood-nerve barrier.

open.q: Which connective tissue sheath surrounding each peripheral nerve fascicle forms the blood-nerve barrier via tight junctions?

questions.q: Following transection of a peripheral axon, what is the triad of morphological changes occurring in the neuronal cell body (chromatolysis)?
options: Cell-body swelling, eccentric nucleus and dispersed Nissl substance
Fusion of adjacent neuronal cell bodies
questions.explain: In central chromatolysis (axon reaction), the neuronal perikaryon swells with fluid, the nucleus shifts eccentrically to the periphery, and Nissl bodies disperse into fine dust as polyribosomes shift toward synthesizing cytoskeletal proteins for axonal regrowth.

open.q: Describe the three characteristic histological changes seen in a neuronal cell body undergoing chromatolysis after axonal injury.
accept: swelling of soma, eccentric nucleus, and dispersion of Nissl bodies
cell swelling, peripheral nucleus, loss of Nissl bodies

questions.q: During Wallerian (anterograde) degeneration distal to a peripheral nerve crush injury, how do Schwann cells facilitate axonal regeneration?
options: Schwann cells form bands of Bungner that guide regenerating axons
They phagocytose the proximal cell body
questions.explain: In the PNS, Schwann cells and recruited macrophages clear myelin debris, and Schwann cells align within the preserved basal lamina tube to form bands of Bungner, secreting neurotrophic factors that guide axonal sprouts.

open.q: Name the longitudinal columns of proliferating Schwann cells formed inside endoneurial tubes that guide regenerating peripheral axons.

questions.q: How can a sensory (dorsal root) ganglion be distinguished histologically from an autonomic (sympathetic) ganglion?
options: Sensory ganglia have pseudounipolar neurons with central nuclei and satellite-cell rings
Sensory ganglia contain multipolar neurons with many synapses
Autonomic ganglia lie within the CNS
questions.explain: Dorsal root and cranial sensory ganglia contain large round pseudounipolar somata with central nuclei surrounded by a complete ring of cuboidal satellite cells and no synapses, whereas autonomic ganglia contain smaller multipolar neurons with eccentric nuclei, incomplete satellite cell investment, and synapses.

open.q: State two histological differences between a dorsal root (sensory) ganglion and an autonomic ganglion.
accept: pseudounipolar central-nucleus neurons with complete satellite cell ring and no synapses vs multipolar eccentric-nucleus neurons with synapses
sensory ganglia have pseudounipolar neurons with central nuclei and no synapses; autonomic have multipolar neurons with eccentric nuclei and synapses

questions.q: Which large, encapsulated mechanoreceptor located deep in the dermis and hypodermis resembles a sliced onion in cross-section and detects high-frequency vibration and deep pressure?
questions.explain: Pacinian corpuscles consist of a single unmyelinated nerve ending surrounded by 20 to 60 concentric lamellae of flattened Schwann-like cells separated by fluid, rapidly adapting to vibration and deep pressure.

open.q: Name the onion-like encapsulated mechanoreceptor in the deep dermis and hypodermis specialized for detecting vibration and deep pressure.

questions.q: Which encapsulated rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor sits within the dermal papillae of glabrous (hairless) skin such as the fingertips and detects fine two-point discriminative touch?
questions.explain: Meissner corpuscles are oval encapsulated receptors located directly beneath the epidermis in dermal papillae of fingertips, palms, and soles, containing horizontally stacked Schwann cell lamellae around spiraling nerve endings.

open.q: Name the oval encapsulated tactile receptor found in the dermal papillae of hairless skin (such as fingertips) that mediates fine discriminative touch.
